title: MATH GAOKAO - 14
description: Authentic-style mathematics problems inspired by China’s Gaokao — build deeper understanding, sharper thinking, and real exam readiness.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the truth value of a conditional statement from the truth values of its components.
questions.question: Let \(p\) be the statement \(3>1\), and let \(q\) be the statement \(4\) is prime. What is the truth value of \(p\rightarrow q\)?
questions.explanation: The statement \(p\) is true because \(3>1\). The statement \(q\) is false because \(4\) is not prime. An implication \(p\rightarrow q\) is false only when \(p\) is true and \(q\) is false. Since \(p\) is true and \(q\) is false, the implication \(p\rightarrow q\) is false.
questions.hint: Recall the truth table for implication, especially the case where the antecedent is true.

questions.concept: Truth Value of a Compound Statement
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a conjunction involving a negation.
questions.question: Suppose \(p\) is false and \(q\) is true. What is the truth value of \(\neg p\land q\)?
questions.explanation:
Since \(p\) is false, \(\neg p\) is true. Since \(q\) is true, both \(\neg p\) and \(q\) are true. A conjunction is true exactly when both parts are true. Therefore,
\[
\neg p\land q
\]
is true.
questions.hint: First determine the truth value of \(\neg p\), then combine it with \(q\).

questions.concept: Truth Value of a Compound Statement
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a compound statement involving disjunction, negation, and conjunction.
questions.question: Let \(p\) be true, \(q\) be false, and \(r\) be true. What is the truth value of \((p\lor q)\land \neg r\)?
questions.explanation:
Since \(p\) is true, the disjunction \(p\lor q\) is true. Since \(r\) is true, \(\neg r\) is false. Therefore,
\[
(p\lor q)\land \neg r
\]
is a conjunction of a true statement and a false statement, which is false.
questions.hint: Evaluate \(p\lor q\) and \(\neg r\) separately before combining them with \(\land\).

questions.learningObjective: Identify a contradiction among given compound statements.
questions.question: Which statement is a contradiction?
questions.explanation:
A contradiction is a statement that is always false. If \(p\) is true, then \(
eg p\) is false, so \(p\land 
eg p\) is false. If \(p\) is false, then \(
eg p\) is true, so \(p\land 
eg p\) is still false. Therefore,
\[
p\land 
eg p
\]

questions.hint: A statement and its negation cannot both be true at the same time.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the truth value of quantified statements over a finite domain.
questions.question: Let \(D=\{1,2,3\}\). Which statement is false?
questions.explanation: For statement A, check each element of \(D\): \(1+1=2\le 4\), \(2+1=3\le 4\), and \(3+1=4\le 4\). Thus A is true. For statement B, the squares of elements of \(D\) are \(1^2=1\), \(2^2=4\), and \(3^2=9\). None equals \(8\), so no element of \(D\) satisfies \(x^2=8\). Therefore, B is false.
questions.hint: Test every element of the finite domain \(D\) in each statement.

questions.concept: Truth Value of a Universal Implication
questions.learningObjective: Determine the truth value of a universally quantified implication.
questions.question: What is the truth value of the statement \(\forall x\in\mathbb{R},\ (x>2\rightarrow x^2>4)\)?
questions.explanation: For every real number \(x\), if \(x>2\), then \(x\) is positive and greater than \(2\). Squaring preserves the inequality for positive numbers, so \(x^2>4\). Therefore, the implication \(x>2\rightarrow x^2>4\) is true for every real number \(x\). Hence the universally quantified statement is true.
questions.hint: Consider what happens to the inequality when a number greater than \(2\) is squared.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the truth value of a biconditional statement from its components.
questions.question: Let \(p\) be the statement “\(5\) is even,” and let \(q\) be the statement “\(7\) is even.” What is the truth value of \(p\leftrightarrow q\)?
questions.explanation:
The statement \(p\) is false because \(5\) is odd. The statement \(q\) is also false because \(7\) is odd. A biconditional \(p\leftrightarrow q\) is true exactly when \(p\) and \(q\) have the same truth value. Since both are false, they have the same truth value. Therefore,
\[
p\leftrightarrow q
\]
is true.
questions.hint: A biconditional is true when both parts have the same truth value.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a statement logically equivalent to an implication.
questions.question: Which statement is logically equivalent to \(p\rightarrow q\)?
questions.explanation:
The implication \(p\rightarrow q\) is false only when \(p\) is true and \(q\) is false. The statement \(\neg p\lor q\) is also false only when \(\neg p\) is false and \(q\) is false, which means \(p\) is true and \(q\) is false. Therefore,
\[
p\rightarrow q\equiv \neg p\lor q.
\]
Option B, \(p\land \neg q\), is actually the negation of \(p\rightarrow q\), not an equivalent statement.
questions.hint: Recall that an implication can be rewritten using “not \(p\) or \(q\).”

questions.learningObjective: Determine which quantified statement is false over a finite domain.
questions.question: Let \(D=\{-1,0,1\}\). Which statement is false?
questions.explanation: For statement A, every element of \(D\) has a nonnegative square: \((-1)^2=1\ge 0\), \(0^2=0\ge 0\), and \(1^2=1\ge 0\). Thus A is true. For statement B, the squares of elements of \(D\) are \(1\), \(0\), and \(1\), none of which is less than \(0\). Therefore, no element of \(D\) satisfies \(x^2<0\), so B is false.
questions.hint: Check the square of each element in the domain \(D\).

questions.concept: Truth Value of a Compound Implication
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a compound implication from given truth values.
questions.question: Suppose \(p\) is true and \(q\) is false. What is the truth value of \((p\lor q)\rightarrow(p\land q)\)?
questions.explanation:
Since \(p\) is true, the disjunction \(p\lor q\) is true. Since \(q\) is false, the conjunction \(p\land q\) is false. Therefore, the statement becomes
\[
\text{true}\rightarrow \text{false}.
\]
An implication is false exactly when its antecedent is true and its consequent is false. Hence
\[
(p\lor q)\rightarrow(p\land q)
\]
is false.
questions.hint: Evaluate the antecedent and the consequent separately before applying the implication rule.
